title: Book 1 — Clio, Chapter 64
paragraphs: Such was the condition of things that Croesus heard was prevailing among the Athenians during this time. As for the Lacedaemonians, he heard that they had escaped from great troubles and had now got the better of the Tegeans in the war. For while Leon and Hegesicles were kings of Sparta, the Lacedaemonians, who had been successful in all their other wars, suffered disaster only in the one they waged against the men of Tegea. Moreover, in earlier times they had had almost the worst laws of any Greeks, both in matters that concerned themselves alone and also in that they had no dealings with strangers. And they made their change to a good constitution of laws in this way: Lycurgus, a man of the Spartans who was held in high repute, came to the Oracle at Delphi, and as he entered the sanctuary of the temple the Pythian prophetess at once spoke as follows:

“See, you are come, O Lycurgus, to this rich shrine of my temple, loved by Zeus and by all who possess the abodes of Olympus. Whether to call you a god, I doubt in my prophetic voices—god or man—but rather a god, I think, O Lycurgus.”
